articles.body: When a Python List Copy Is Only Half a Copy You used .copy() , but changing your copied data still affected the original. Did the copy fail? The answer depends on what is inside your list. A shallow copy creates a new outer list, while its elements still refer to the same objects. Let’s explore this through a weekly schedule. 1. Adding a day keeps the original unchanged schedule = [ [ "Monday" , "Python" ] , [ "Tuesday" , "SQL" ] , ] revised = schedule . copy ( ) revised . append ( [ "Wednesday" , "Git" ] ) print ( len ( schedule ) ) print ( len ( revised ) ) Output: 2 3 Calling .copy() created a separate outer list. Appending a new entry changes only revised . So far, the copy behaves exactly as you might expect. 2.

articles.title: Cutover Needs a No-Go: Microsoft, Workday, the FAA, and Starship Flight 15
articles.excerpt: These four events landed in the same mid-November 2026 window. Nothing public connects them, and I am not suggesting a link. What they share is a lesson about gates, verification and change discipline…
articles.body: These four events landed in the same mid-November 2026 window. Nothing public connects them, and I am not suggesting a link. What they share is a lesson about gates, verification and change discipline. Things fail at cutovers, at tests that touch production, and in old infrastructure that is finally being changed. One of the four shows the opposite pattern: an automated no-go that refused to proceed. I build MigrateForge in Coimbatore: a system that moves PHP applications to Java 21 / Spring Boot and keeps cutover blocked until recorded user journeys match on both sides. That is not a claim that it would have prevented any of these incidents. It is about applying the same discipline to a software cutover. Microsoft 365: the checker was in the failure path Starting shortly before 1 p.m.

articles.title: Cursor's breach chain started in plain-text agent traces: 23,276 public repos carry the same leak
articles.excerpt: Cursor published its final incident report on November 13, two weeks after a malicious copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension appeared in its VS Code extension marketplace. I read the whole thing.…
articles.body: Cursor published its final incident report on November 13, two weeks after a malicious copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension appeared in its VS Code extension marketplace. I read the whole thing. The interesting part is not the extension. It is the first link in the chain. The chain, in five steps The report reconstructs the attack like this: An attacker obtained an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks, an inference provider. The key was exposed on Fireworks' side. With that key, the attacker copied data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor used to share training data with Fireworks. The bucket held coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted.

articles.title: Docker layer caching not working: read the CACHED count first
articles.excerpt: When Docker layer caching GitHub Actions not working is the complaint, the clock is a bad witness and the build log is a good one: a build that reuses nothing and a build that reuses everything can be…
articles.body: When Docker layer caching GitHub Actions not working is the complaint, the clock is a bad witness and the build log is a good one: a build that reuses nothing and a build that reuses everything can be seconds apart, and the number that separates them is how many steps printed CACHED . On a runner we measured, the same image came back with 5 cached steps when the cache was wired correctly and 0 in every one of the four ways it can quietly fail. One image, one runner, a freshly created builder before every build. Cached step counts and seconds from job-m.sh on a latchkey-small runner, 2026-09-20. A layer cache that is configured and not working produces a build that looks entirely normal. Nothing fails, the workflow is green, and the only evidence is that every step ran again.

articles.body: I built a small meeting recorder that runs as a PWA in Edge. It records the screen, the other people's voices (system audio) and my own microphone into one MP4. This post is about how it works, including the parts that took me a while to get right. What I wanted: one MP4 with screen + system audio + mic hours of recording without holding the file in memory files that seek properly in any player Setup: Windows 11, Microsoft Edge (Chrome behaves the same). APIs: getDisplayMedia , Web Audio, MediaStreamTrackProcessor , WebCodecs, File System Access API. MP4 muxing is done by mp4-muxer (MIT). Why not MediaRecorder MediaRecorder is the easy option, but I wanted control over a few things: Seeking. WebM files from MediaRecorder have no duration or cues, so some players can't seek in them.

articles.title: Scanning 3.8B Lines of Code Across 7,135 GitHub Repos: Measuring Cognitive Ownership & PR Review Risk
articles.excerpt: AI-assisted code generation is not inherently a software defect. Most high-performing engineering teams use coding assistants every day for boilerplate, migrations, and test scaffolding. For CTOs, CIS…
articles.body: AI-assisted code generation is not inherently a software defect. Most high-performing engineering teams use coding assistants every day for boilerplate, migrations, and test scaffolding. For CTOs, CISOs, and Staff Reviewers, the real systems problem is review velocity versus generation throughput : when diff volume scales faster than human review bandwidth, teams risk losing cognitive ownership , missing unverified third-party dependencies , and merging over-engineered abstractions . To move this conversation away from guesswork and noisy probabilistic "AI detectors," we have been tracking deterministic static-analysis heuristics across 7,135 open-source GitHub repositories (~ 3.8 billion lines of code and 16.0 million pattern hits ) on SlopCodeMonitor .

articles.body: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articles.excerpt: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Hele…
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely .

articles.title: Why did Starship Flight 15 booster abort 'chopsticks' landing catch? SpaceX still investigating (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13) during the Starship Flight 15 test.
articles.body: Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that." SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster. The giant Starship rocket , a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.
